title: A Lovely, Silent, Well-Behaved Way To End Each Day ch-day/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin revisits and refines a strategy he has written about before: ending each day or period with one minute of silence to counteract the chaos and rising misbehavior common during dismissal wind-down. His new addition is to give students a specific focal point during that minute, since focusing the mind on one thing has a calming effect similar to meditation. He offers three objects of focus that have worked especially well in his experience: deep diaphragmatic breathing, a moment of gratefulness for something about the class, and reflection on one area of personal improvement that day. Each is described with brief, practical instructions teachers can use directly. He closes by encouraging teachers to experiment with other points of focus suited to their grade level, emphasizing that the specific choice matters less than making the minute of stillness a consistent, expected part of the daily dismissal routine.
points: Ending the day with one minute of focused silence counters the chaos and rising misbehavior typical of dismissal wind-down.
Giving students a specific object of attention—rather than open silence—amplifies the calming, meditation-like effect.
Three effective focal points are offered: diaphragmatic breathing, gratefulness, and reflecting on a personal improvement.
The practice quiets students, reduces last-minute misbehavior, and sends them off calm and content.
Consistency matters more than the specific focal point chosen; it should become a regular, anticipated part of the dismissal routine.
quotes: This underscores the importance of starting your wind-down early, of giving yourself enough time to calmly get your students ready to go.
Focusing the mind on a single sound, movement, or thought has a unique way of calming excitability, restlessness, tension, and stress. In fact, it’s the basis behind the practice of meditation.
Sit up straight (or stand) and place your hand on your stomach as you expand on the inhale and contract on the exhale.
Have them relive that experience by visualizing it, savoring it, and remembering how it felt.
In this way, that brief time of stillness and reflection will become a calming touchstone your students look forward to every day.
